title: Kubernetes pods restart even though application logs look healthy
description: Diagnose silent pod restarts caused by OOMKill, liveness probe failures, or node pressure when application logs show no errors.

data.text: The application logs are clean. No exceptions, no stack traces, no warnings. But the pod has restarted twelve times in the last hour. Kubernetes is killing the container for reasons the application never sees: an out-of-memory kill at the kernel level, a liveness probe that fails during a GC pause, or node pressure that evicts the pod without the application logging anything. The fix is not in your code—it is in the pod spec, the resource limits, and the probe configuration.

data.title: Core concepts
items: OOMKilled: the Linux OOM killer terminates the process when it exceeds its memory limit (exit code 137)
Liveness probe: a Kubernetes check that restarts the container when it fails
Startup probe: delays liveness and readiness checks until the application has finished initializing
Node pressure eviction: the kubelet evicts pods when a node runs low on memory or disk
QoS class: Kubernetes classifies pods as Guaranteed, Burstable, or BestEffort based on resource requests and limits

terms.definition: A container exit code (137) indicating the Linux OOM killer terminated the process because it exceeded its memory limit.
A Kubernetes probe that determines whether a container is running. If it fails, the kubelet kills and restarts the container.
A probe that delays liveness and readiness checks until the application has finished starting up, preventing premature restarts.
The kubelet evicts pods when a node runs low on memory, disk, or inodes, prioritizing by QoS class.

items: Memory limit is lower than the application actual working set, causing OOMKill
Liveness probe is too aggressive and fails during legitimate startup or GC pauses
Health check endpoint is not implemented or returns 500 during initialization
Node pressure evicts pods when the node runs low on memory or disk
Process receives a SIGTERM from the kubelet and exits before flushing logs
Startup probe is missing, so liveness checks run before the app is ready

cards.title: OOMKilled
cards.description: The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed the process.
cons: May not happen under low traffic

cards.title: Liveness Probe Failure
cards.description: The health check endpoint returned a non-success response, so Kubernetes restarted the container.
cons: May be caused by transient slowness

cards.title: Node Pressure Eviction
cards.description: The node ran low on memory or disk and evicted pods to free resources.
pros: Eviction events appear in node status
Can be tuned with QoS classes
cons: Pod may be rescheduled on another node

data.caption: Kubernetes pod restart decision flow
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Container Running] --> B{Probe Check}
    B -->|Liveness Fail| C[Kill Container]
    B -->|Readiness Fail| D[Remove from Service]
    B -->|Pass| E[Continue]
    C --> F[Restart Container]
    F --> G{Startup Probe?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Wait for Startup]
    G -->|No| I[Run Liveness Immediately]
    H --> J[App Ready]
    I --> J

items: Run kubectl describe pod and check Last State Reason and Exit Code.
If OOMKilled, increase the memory limit or reduce the application working set.
If liveness probe failure, verify the health endpoint is fast, reliable, and does not depend on downstream services.
Add a startup probe with a generous failure threshold to delay liveness checks until the app is ready.
Review node allocatable and eviction thresholds with kubectl describe node.
Add resource requests and limits to stabilize scheduling and QoS class.

data.title: Probes should not depend on downstreams
data.text: Liveness probes must be independent. If your health check calls a database or external API, a downstream outage will cause your pod to restart even when the application is healthy.

items: Define realistic memory requests and limits based on load-test profiling, not guesses
Use a startup probe for applications with slow initialization or JIT compilation
Keep liveness probes lightweight: check a local endpoint or thread state, not dependencies
Set container lifecycle preStop hooks to allow graceful shutdown and log flushing
Monitor OOMKill events with a Prometheus rule or Datadog monitor
Run chaos experiments that induce memory pressure to validate restart behavior

items.question: Why does the app log show no errors before restart?
items.answer: OOMKill terminates the process at the kernel level. The application never gets a chance to log the event. Check pod status and node events instead of container logs.

items.question: Should I increase the liveness probe failure threshold?
items.answer: Increase the threshold or add a startup probe if the app has slow or variable startup times. Do not mask a genuinely unhealthy endpoint by making the probe too lenient.

data.title: Investigate a crashing pod
data.description: A .NET API pod restarts every few minutes. kubectl logs shows no errors. Diagnose using kubectl describe, events, and metrics.
steps: Check the pod Last State Reason and Exit Code
Inspect node memory pressure and OOM events
Review container memory limits and actual usage with kubectl top
Examine the liveness probe configuration and endpoint implementation
Implement a fix: increase limits, add startup probe, or fix the health check
data.expectedOutcome: You should identify whether the root cause is OOMKill, probe failure, or node eviction and implement a targeted fix.

data.title: Summary
points: OOMKill leaves no application logs; check pod status and exit codes
Use startup probes to protect slow-initializing apps from premature restarts
Keep liveness probes independent of external dependencies
Set memory limits based on profiling data, not arbitrary values
Monitor restart counts and OOMKill events as a first-class health signal
data.takeaway: Healthy application logs do not prove the container is healthy. Kubernetes probes and resource limits are the real source of truth for pod lifecycle.
